prompt.context: Your client eNP & Co is a mid-size department store (something like Macy's) that has mainly two categories: apparel and home décor. The department store has seen declining profitability and has called McKinsey to understand what its strategic next steps should be. The client has only one store, located in Chicago. Home décor covers all categories of home furnishing products. Apparel covers Men's, Women's, and Children's apparel.
prompt.question: What are the strategic next steps for eNP & Co given its declining profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Which category is driving the profitability decline?
clarifying_info.a: The apparel business is seeing declining profitability.

clarifying_info.q: How is the industry performing overall?
clarifying_info.a: The industry for both home décor and apparel is growing at a steady rate of 5% to 10%.

clarifying_info.q: Does eNP sell through any online channels?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has only been selling through traditional (brick-and-mortar) sales channels.

clarifying_info.q: What are the latest consumer trends?
clarifying_info.a: People are shopping online increasingly. People do not like to travel long distances to buy apparel. The store is located in an area similar to where Walmart and K-Mart are located; consumers prefer to shop closer to downtown.

exhibits.title: Profitability Data by Category
exhibits.shows: A table providing gross margin per customer, number of customers per week, number of purchases per customer, and total square footage for each category (Home Décor, Women's Apparel, Men's Apparel, Children's Apparel), plus the store's annual fixed costs.

framework: Identify which category drives profitability decline (Home Décor vs. Apparel sub-categories)
Analyze industry context: industry-wide issue or company-specific? Competitive landscape? Consumer trends?
Break down revenue and cost structure by category: gross margin per sq ft vs. fixed cost per sq ft
Assess organizational and operational changes: suppliers, management, marketing spend allocation, product mix
Evaluate distribution channels: absence of online channel given shifting consumer behavior
Examine store-level factors: location, foot traffic, in-store placement, product assortment
Develop strategic alternatives and recommendation (divest category, expand online, relocate)

questions.prompt: What are the key drivers we should evaluate to diagnose eNP's declining profitability?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify the need to isolate which category (apparel vs. home décor) is underperforming, then drill into: (1) industry trends and competitive landscape, (2) revenue/cost breakdown by sub-category, (3) organizational changes (management, suppliers, marketing allocation), (4) channel gaps (no online presence), and (5) store-level factors (location, assortment, placement). Bonus for noting the mismatch between consumer behavior (online shopping, downtown preference) and eNP's positioning.

questions.prompt: What is the profitability (gross margin) per square foot for each category?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual gross margin for each category using: Annual Gross Margin = Gross Margin per Customer × Customers per Week × Purchases per Customer × 52 weeks. Then divide by square footage. Compare result to fixed cost per square foot ($155) to identify unprofitable categories. Children's Apparel gross margin per sq ft ($111) is below the fixed cost per sq ft ($155), signaling it is the problem area.

math.setup: Annual Gross Margin per category = (Gross Margin per Customer) × (Customers/week) × (Purchases/customer) × 52. Gross Margin per sq ft = Annual Gross Margin ÷ sq footage. Fixed Cost per sq ft = Total Fixed Costs ÷ Total sq footage = $775,000 ÷ 5,000 = $155.
math.answer: Children's Apparel gross margin per sq ft = $111, which is below the fixed cost per sq ft of $155. All other categories exceed the fixed cost threshold (Home Décor $233, Women's $312, Men's $222). Children's Apparel is the underperforming category.

questions.prompt: How many more customers of Children's Apparel should eNP sell to per week to achieve a target average profitability of $200 per square foot?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work backward from the target gross margin per sq ft to find the required number of customers, then compute the incremental increase. Should note that a ~80% increase in customers is a very ambitious target and flag feasibility concerns.

math.setup: Target gross margin per sq ft for Children's Apparel = $200. Total desired annual gross margin = $200 × 750 sq ft = $150,000. Required customers per week = $150,000 ÷ (Gross Margin per Customer × Purchases per Customer × 52 weeks).
steps: Increase needed = 36 − 20 = 16 additional customers per week
math.answer: eNP needs 16 more customers per week (total of 36), representing an 80% increase. The large required increase raises serious feasibility questions.

questions.prompt: Why do you think the Children's Apparel category is not performing well?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming question. Strong answers span customer behavior, product assortment, in-store execution, marketing, and location factors.

brainstorming.prompt: Why do you think the Children's Apparel category is not doing well?

categories.name: Customer behavior & channel
ideas: Young parents do not have time to visit stores; they buy children's clothes online
People who visit for home décor do not intend to buy children's clothing
The store location is not ideal for a full family shopping trip

categories.name: Product assortment & merchandising
ideas: eNP does not carry the right categories or latest styles of children's apparel
Parents prefer stylish/expensive children's clothes; eNP's assortment may not match
Children's Apparel is not strategically placed inside the store to drive traffic or impulse purchase

categories.name: Marketing & promotion
ideas: eNP relies on traditional media and has not embraced social media, missing young-parent audiences
Marketing budget is disproportionately allocated to home décor rather than children's apparel

categories.name: Location & competition
ideas: Store is in a Walmart/K-Mart-style location, not ideal for family apparel shopping
Consumers prefer downtown shopping; better-located competitors capture the family segment

recommendation: Option 1: Divest from Children's Apparel only — it is unprofitable and an unintuitive fit in a home décor-anchored store; reallocate floor space to profitable categories.
Option 2: Divest from all Apparel — home décor is the most profitable segment; position eNP as an exclusive home décor destination, eliminating consumer confusion.
Option 3: Create a separate apparel store (possibly a sub-brand) in a better city-center location and launch an online channel to serve the digital-first apparel shopper.
risks: Divestiture from apparel reduces cross-sell opportunities between categories
Focusing solely on home décor means customers may not visit frequently enough to sustain foot traffic
A new city-center store increases rent and other fixed costs, and intensifies competition
next_steps: Conduct detailed customer research to quantify online shopping behavior among target segments
Model financial impact of each divestiture option with updated rent/cost assumptions
Pilot an online sales channel for apparel to test demand before committing to a physical sub-brand
Evaluate potential to reallocate freed floor space to higher-margin home décor sub-categories
